title: Bridging Fairness and Explainability: Can Input-Based Explanations Promote Fairness in Hate Speech Detection?
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: One study decomposes an analysis into three research questions, each tested with an explanation-based procedure on the same example inputs.
layout: 3 panels split by dashed lines, left-to-right flow, token-highlighted example sentences
description: The figure is split into three labeled panels, RQ1 Bias Detection (top left), RQ3 Bias Mitigation (bottom left) and RQ2 Fair Model Selection (right), separated by dashed lines. RQ1 and RQ3 show example hateful or neutral sentences. Green shading marks each word's contribution to the prediction, and blue boxes mark sensitive tokens such as 'Muslims', 'White' and 'She'. RQ1 adds columns for the model's prediction (emoji), individual unfairness and sensitive-token reliance, plus a correlation value of 0.56. RQ3 shows reliance scores before and after a large red 'Training' arrow, labeled with sensitive-token reliance regularization. RQ2 sends test and validation sentence sets through stacked, color-coded models into fairness ranks and explanation-based ranks. A bracket links the two ranks to a rank correlation of 0.42 and MRR@1 of 0.50. The eye goes first to the green-highlighted sentences.
caption: Workflow diagram illustrating the processes used to address each research question. Sensitive tokens are shown in blue boxes, and the intensity of the green shading reflects each word’s contribution to the model’s prediction.
abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) models often replicate or amplify social bias from training data, raising concerns about fairness. At the same time, their black-box nature makes it difficult for users to recognize biased predictions and for developers to effectively mitigate them. While some studies suggest that input-based explanations can help detect and mitigate bias, others question their reliability in ensuring fairness. Existing research on explainability in fair NLP has been predominantly qualitative, with limited large-scale quantitative analysis. In this work, we conduct the first systematic study of the relationship between explainability and fairness in hate speech detection, focusing on both encoder- and decoder-only models. We examine three key dimensions: (1) identifying biased predictions, (2) selecting fair models, and (3) mitigating bias during model training. Our findings show that input-based explanations can effectively detect biased predictions and serve as useful supervision for reducing bias during training, but they are unreliable for selecting fair models among candidates.Our code is available at https://github.com/Ewanwong/fairness_x_explainability.
